12494-note-book-of-anton-chekhov:
Translated by S. S. Koteliansky and Leonard Woolf in 1921, Chekhov's Note-Book gathers notes, themes and sketches for works he intended to write. Papers found after his death bore a cover inscribed Themes, thoughts, notes, and fragments, and his wife, Olga Knipper-Chekhov, also kept a notebook of themes, quotations and future work.

Chekhov struck out material once used, and recopied much of it into a special copy book, a sign of the value he placed on it. Entries run from diary notes of 1896, such as a neighbour's tale of the poet Fet, to seeds of stories and plays. The volume lets readers watch a master gather raw life, in jottings, before art reshaped it.
17222-water-baptism-a-pagan-and-jewish-r:
James H. Moon's 1902 tract argues that water baptism is a pagan and Jewish rite, not a Christian one, proven by scripture and history. He opens with the commission: did Christ command water baptism at all? Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, and Peter each give the command in different words, Moon notes, and seven accounts of the commission appear in the New Testament.

Moon seeks a reading that harmonizes all seven, rather than pinning faith to one version alone. He adds lives of saints never baptized with water as proof for his case. The tract speaks for a Quaker-like view of inward baptism. Readers of baptism debates will find a plain, earnest argument, stated with care and full scripture talk.
21256-travels-through-the-south-of-franc:
Lieutenant-Colonel Pinkney of the North American Native Rangers travelled through southern France in 1807 and 1808. His route, he says, was never performed before: along the banks of the Loire, the Isère, and the Garonne. He travelled with the French government's permission. His book appeared in London in 1809.

He sails from Baltimore to Liverpool, crosses to Calais, buys a Norman horse, and posts south through Boulogne. Markets, prices, cottages, dances on the green, and French domestic economy fill his chapters. An American officer's view of Napoleonic France, written for English readers curious about the enemy's country, is the book's special value.
24343-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-46:
William and Robert Chambers edited this weekly journal, and this number is dated Saturday, November 6, 1852, priced at a penny halfpenny. It opens with The Managing Partner, a satiric essay on a busybody who appoints herself manager of other people's affairs without belonging to any of them. Matrimony is only one department of her general business. Why she has a hand in so many concerns is as mysterious as the origin of the poet, or of black Topsy, who was not born at all but growed.

The managing partner was managing from infancy, screaming lustily in the nurse's arms when things went wrong, her screams mere substitutes for words. When language came, the screaming stopped but the managing did not, directing play rather than playing it, and distributing parts to companions. Readers get a sharp Victorian sketch of a woman who runs everything.
25278-amateur-gardencraft-a-book-for-the: Eben E. Rexford's Amateur Gardencraft, published by Lippincott in 1912 with 34 illustrations, is known here only from its title page and the opening of its introduction. The text supplied promises clear instructions from personal experience for home-owners improving their grounds, and praises home beautifying as a duty and a gospel of beauty. No further chapters are present in the sample.
27078-senate-resolution-6-41st-congress-:
Senate bill S. 6 of the 41st Congress, introduced March 5, 1869, by Mr. Anthony, proposes to provide stationery for Congress and the several departments. Read twice and ordered printed, the bill sets out a new system for buying paper and supplies.

Under its terms, heads of each executive and judicial department would estimate a year's stationery needs. They would send them to the Congressional Printer, who would advertise for sealed proposals and buy under set rules. The bill also asks the printer to report each session's paper needs to the Joint Committee on Public Printing.
491-rezanov:
Gertrude Atherton retells the romance of Nikolai Rezanov, a Russian noble who sailed to Spanish California, in this historical novel. Rezanov, seeking trade and an alliance, falls in love with Concha Arguello, daughter of the San Francisco commandant. Their brief courtship, cut short by his death on the road home, became California legend.

Atherton writes with warm, vivid style, praising the tale's primeval, almost ballad quality. An introduction by William Marion Reedy calls it her most charming book. The novel blends fact and fancy into a poignant tale of love across empires, faiths, and seas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-stra:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Strahov describes a Premonstratensian abbey at Prague. Henry Zdik of Olmütz, John of Prague, and Prince Ladislaus the Second founded it in 1149. Monks from Steinfeld near Cologne formed the colony, and Gero, a canon of Cologne, became first abbot.

Strahov flourished so quickly that members were soon made bishops of Prague. Through the twelfth, thirteenth and fourteenth centuries its abbots took keen interest in the kingdom's public affairs. Fire destroyed the abbey in October 1259, but Abbot John the First built a magnificent new church. Under Charles the Fourth it flourished again before Hussites fired and looted it in May 1420.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-martinov:
John Martinov was a Russian Jesuit scholar who reached his countrymen only through his writings. Born in 1821, he studied with distinction at St. Petersburg, tutored Count Schouvalov's children on a European tour, met Father de Ravignan in France, and was received into the Catholic Church. Barred from returning to Russia, he entered the French Jesuits in 1845.

Like Father Gagarin, with whom he often worked, Martinov devoted himself to literature and correspondence, writing for the Revue des Questions Historiques, Polybiblion, and Etudes Religieuses. Called to Rome by Pius IX to serve as papal theologian for the Vatican Council, he later advised the Propaganda on Oriental rites. His fifty-two works in Russian, French, and Latin include the Graeco-Slavonic Church Year in the Bollandist Acta Sanctorum, and he died at Cannes in 1894.
doe-osti-3023579-evaluateflux-varpow-var: DIF3D got utility-revved-1, and this DOE text covers EvaluateFlux and VARPOW. The pages detail the program findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The revision was 1. The data were nuclear. The DIF3D were programs. The 1 was Rev.

fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in:
Phoenix opened this Federal Bureau of Investigation summary on November 16, 2001, for the case of Rayed Mohammed Abdullah. A full investigation had been cleared on October 5, 2001. The case grew out of facts found in the probe into the September 11 hijackings.

The sampled pages map how the hijacker teams crossed paths in Maryland. Men from the Flight 77 team used computers at a copy shop in Laurel and met around Laurel and College Park. Ziad Jarrah, of Flight 93, was seen with them and used some of the same hotels. On August 13 and 14, 2001, Nawaf Al Hazmi and Hani Hanjour went to Las Vegas at the same time as Mohamed Atta. The summary treats these shared places as threads worth pulling.

Phoenix prepared this Federal Bureau of Investigation summary, dated November 8, 2002, on Fahad Salem Awadh Mohsin-Al-Wahedi. His name opens the file, with a short form, Fahad Salem Al Wahedi, given too. The office of origin is Phoenix, and the case head names Bin Laden and Al Qaeda.

The base the summary lays out is Al Qaeda itself. It says the group, led by Usama Bin Laden, had declared holy war on the United States. It counts three fatwas that called on Muslims to kill Americans, in or out of uniform. It dates the name Al Qaeda, the Base, to 1988. Later pages give the group's reach: about twelve camps in Afghanistan, as many as 5,000 men trained, and cells in fifty countries.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Yuri Orlov, who died in 2020 at ninety-six, was both a serious physicist and a founder of the Soviet human rights movement. Svetlana Savranskaya and Tom Blanton compiled this memorial briefing book, number 724. Orlov founded the Moscow Helsinki Group, which monitored Soviet compliance with human rights promises.

He proposed glasnost, openness, almost fifteen years before Gorbachev made it policy. For that work he paid with prison and exile. The memorial builds on an earlier 2014 briefing book on Orlov, updated at his death. It preserves the record of a scientist who treated truth telling as a method, in physics and in politics alike.
nasa-tm-19720016358-preliminary-noise-te:
Meyer Reshotko, William A Olsen, and Robert G Dorsch of the Lewis Research Center reported these noise tests in March 1972, as NASA TM X-68032. They studied placing the engine over the wing of a short takeoff aircraft. The wing itself might then shield people below from jet noise. Cities near small airports needed such quiet designs. This first report covers the landing flap settings. The flaps sat at thirty and sixty degrees.

A small wing section model stood in for the full aircraft. Its chord measured about thirty two centimeters. Simulated engine exhaust flowed over the wing and flaps. The team recorded the sound the setup produced in each position. Engine over wing designs promised shielding plus blown lift. These early tests began measuring whether the promise held.
note-book-of-anton-chekhov:
Anton Chekhov's Note-Book came out in English in 1921, translated by S. S. Koteliansky and Leonard Woolf. A note up front explains the material: themes, thoughts, and fragments for works Chekhov meant to write. Sheets in a special cover held them among his papers. His wife kept the note-book itself.

Chekhov struck out any note once he used it in a work. He recopied most of the rest into a special copy book, which shows the worth he set on them. Diary pages from 1896 follow the notes. One tale tells of a poet who always spat at the University when his carriage passed it in Moscow.
rezanov:
Gertrude Atherton's novel Rezanov is introduced here by William Marion Reedy, who calls it the best of her books. Atherton, a Californian by birth and home, writes with a grasp of character and a warm, glowing style, Reedy says. He finds her a realist saturated with the romance of California.

Reedy calls the book a simple story, almost an incident, and not so much a novel as a historical idyll. It was first published in 1906, though few agreed with his high praise at the time. He finds in it a strange, primeval quality like Aucassin and Nicolette, and a tenderness that makes it unforgettable.
water-baptism-a-pagan-and-jewish-rite-bu:
James H. Moon of Fallsington, Pennsylvania, published Water Baptism in 1902 to argue that the rite is pagan and Jewish, but not Christian. His subtitle claims the case is proven by scripture and history, and confirmed by the lives of saints who were never baptized with water. The first chapter, called The Commission, asks a plain question: did Christ ever tell his disciples to baptize with water?

Moon bids readers search the New Testament and compare the answers. The four evangelists and Peter, he says, give Christ's charge to his apostles in very different words, and seven distinct accounts of the commission stand in the text. The usual proof text, in Matthew, he distrusts, since that gospel itself shows signs of being written long after the events. His book builds a case from those clashing reports, aimed at readers who take baptism with water as a clear command.
